subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide (and fall in pH):
options: Has no effect on oxygen affinity
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given partial pressure
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing haemoglobin's affinity
questions.explain: Higher CO2 lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues.

questions.q: A plant cell becomes plasmolysed when placed in a concentrated salt solution because:
options: the cell wall ruptures
water enters the cell, pushing the membrane against the wall
water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall
salt is actively pumped out of the cell
questions.explain: The external solution has a lower (more negative) water potential, so water leaves the cell and the plasma membrane pulls away from the wall.

options: The exchange of oxygen for chloride at the alveoli
The active uptake of chloride during the Bohr effect
The movement of Cl- into red blood cells to balance the charge as HCO3- leaves
The loss of Cl- from plasma during digestion
questions.explain: As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of red cells, chloride ions move in to maintain electrical neutrality.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
have no effect on the curve
lower the Vmax that can be reached
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump in co-transport maintains a low intracellular Na+ concentration by:
options: pumping glucose out of the cell
allowing Na+ to diffuse passively out
actively pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP
breaking down the cell membrane
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ ATPase actively exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP, creating the Na+ gradient that powers glucose co-transport.

questions.q: An advantage of using immobilised enzymes in industrial processes is that:
options: they have a lower optimum temperature
the enzyme can be recovered and reused, and does not contaminate the product
they require no substrate
they react faster than free enzymes in all cases
questions.explain: Immobilising enzymes on an inert support allows easy recovery, reuse and a product free of enzyme contamination, often with greater thermal stability.

questions.q: At high substrate concentration with fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of reaction plateaus because:
options: the enzyme has denatured
all active sites are occupied so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
the pH has changed
the substrate is used up
questions.explain: When substrate is in excess, every active site is continually occupied, so the number of enzyme molecules limits the rate.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
Carbonic acid in the plasma
Carbaminohaemoglobin
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: Two cells are in contact: cell A has a water potential of -400 kPa and cell B has -750 kPa. Water will move:
options: from cell A to cell B
in both directions equally with no net movement
from cell B to cell A
not at all because the cells are isolated
questions.explain: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) one, i.e. from A (-400) to B (-750).

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
options: A rise in temperature
An increase in atmospheric humidity
An increase in air movement (wind)
A decrease in atmospheric humidity
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.

questions.q: As an organism increases in size, why does it require a specialised exchange surface?
options: Its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, slowing diffusion
Volume increases more slowly than surface area
Larger cells respire anaerobically and need no oxygen
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases, so diffusion across the body surface cannot meet metabolic demand
questions.explain: As size increases, volume rises faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls and the body surface alone cannot supply the cells.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
It transports water to the stomata
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.
